topic.name: Integrating Rational Functions Using Partial Fractions

question.explanation:
We'll work out the indefinite integral first and then proceed with the definite integral.

First, we note that a denominator of the integrand can be factored as \[ x^2-1 = (x-1)(x+1). \]

So the integrand can be converted into a sum of partial fractions, \begin{align*} \dfrac{1}{x^2-1} &= \dfrac{1}{(x-1)(x+1)} = \dfrac{A}{(x+1)} +\dfrac{B}{(x-1)}, \end{align*}

which gives \[ 1 = A(x-1) +B(x+1). \]

Plugging in $x=1,$ we can eliminate $A$ and solve for $B\mathbin{:}$ \begin{align*} 1 &= A(1-1) +B(1+1)\\[3pt] 1 &= 2B \\[3pt] B&=\dfrac 12 \end{align*}

On the other hand, plugging in $x=-1,$ we can eliminate $B$ and solve for $A\mathbin{:}$ \begin{align*} 1 &= A(-1-1) +B(-1+1)\\[3pt] 1 &= -2A \\[3pt] A&=-\dfrac 12 \end{align*}

Therefore,

\[ \dfrac{1}{x^2-1} = -\dfrac{1}{2(x+1)} +\dfrac{1}{2(x-1)}. \]

Now, we integrate, and we get

\begin{align*} \int \dfrac{1}{x^2-1} \,\textrm{d}x &= \int \left(-\dfrac{1}{2(x+1)} +\dfrac{1}{2(x-1)} \right) \textrm{d}x\\[5pt] &= \dfrac{1}{2}\int \dfrac{1}{x-1} \,\textrm{d}x-\dfrac{1}{2}\int \dfrac{1}{x+1} \,\textrm{d}x\\[5pt] &= \dfrac{1}{2}\ln \left\vert {x-1}\right\vert-\dfrac{1}{2}\ln \left\vert {x+1}\right\vert+C. \end{align*}

We can simplify the result using the laws of logarithms, as follows:

\begin{align*} \int \dfrac{\textrm{d}x}{x^2-1} \,\textrm{d}x &= \dfrac{1}{2}\ln \left\vert {x-1}\right\vert-\dfrac{1}{2}\ln \left\vert {x+1}\right\vert+C\\[5pt] &= \dfrac{1}{2}\ln \left\vert \dfrac{x-1}{x+1} \right\vert + C \end{align*}

Finally, the definite integral is

\begin{align*} \int_2^3 \dfrac{1}{x^2-1} \,\textrm{d}x &= \dfrac{1}{2} \ln \left\vert \dfrac{x-1}{x+1} \right\vert \Bigg|_2^3 \\[5pt] &=\dfrac{1}{2}\left( \ln \left(\dfrac 12\right) - \ln \left(\dfrac 13\right) \right)\\[5pt] &=\dfrac{1}{2}\ln \left(\dfrac{1}{2} \cdot \dfrac{3}{1} \right)\\[5pt] &=\dfrac{1}{2}\ln \left(\dfrac{3}{2} \right). \end{align*}

example.title: Calculating a Definite Integral of a Rational Function Using Partial Fractions

question.explanation:
We'll work out the indefinite integral first and then proceed with the definite integral.

First, we note that a denominator of the integrand can be factored as \[ 4x^2+5x+1= (4x+1)(x+1). \]

So the integrand can be converted into a sum of partial fractions, \begin{align*} \dfrac{2x + 1}{4x^2+5x+1}&= \dfrac{2x + 1}{(4x+1)(x+1)} = \dfrac{A}{4x+1} + \dfrac{B}{x+1}, \end{align*}

which gives \[ 2x + 1 = A(x+1) +B(4x+1). \]

Plugging in $x=-1,$ we can eliminate $A$ and solve for $B\mathbin{:}$ \begin{align*} 2(-1) + 1 & = A(-1+1) +B(4(-1)+1)\\[3pt] -1 & = -3B \\[3pt] B & = \dfrac{1}{3} \end{align*}

On the other hand, plugging in $x = -\dfrac{1}{4},$ we can eliminate $B$ and solve for $A\mathbin{:}$ \begin{align*} 2\left(-\dfrac 14\right) + 1& = A\left(-\dfrac 14+1\right) +B\left(4\left(-\dfrac 14\right)+1\right)\\[5pt] \dfrac{1}{2} & = \dfrac{3}{4}A \\[5pt] A & = \dfrac{2}{3} \end{align*}

Therefore, \[ \dfrac{2x + 1}{4x^2+5x+1} = \dfrac{2}{3(4x+1)} + \dfrac{1}{3(x+1)}. \]

Now, we integrate, and we get

\[ \begin{align*} \int \dfrac{2x + 1}{4x^2+5x+1} \, \textrm{d}x & = \int \left(\dfrac{2}{3(4x+1)} + \dfrac{1}{3(x+1)} \right) \textrm{d}x\\[5pt] &= \dfrac{1}{6}\int \dfrac{4}{4x+1} \, \textrm{d}x + \dfrac{1}{3}\int \dfrac{1}{x+1} \,\textrm{d}x\\[5pt] &= \dfrac{1}{6}\ln |4x+1| + \dfrac{1}{3}\ln | x+1| + C. \end{align*} \]

We can simplify the result using the laws of logarithms, as follows:

\begin{align*} \int \dfrac{2x + 1}{4x^2+5x+1}\,\textrm{d}x &= \dfrac{1}{6}\ln |4x+1| + \dfrac{1}{3}\ln | x+1| + C\\[5pt] &= \dfrac{1}{3}\ln \sqrt{4x+1} + \dfrac{1}{3}\ln | x+1| + C\\[5pt] & = \dfrac{1}{3}\ln\left| (x+1)\sqrt{4x + 1} \right| + C \end{align*}

Finally, the definite integral is \[ \begin{align*} \int_{0}^{2}\dfrac{2x + 1}{4x^2+5x+1} \, \textrm{d}x & = \dfrac{1}{3}\ln\left| (x+1)\sqrt{4x + 1} \right| \Bigg|_{0}^{2} \\[5pt] & = \dfrac{1}{3}\ln(3\sqrt{9})\\[5pt] & = \dfrac{1}{3}\ln(3^2)\\[5pt] & = \dfrac{2}{3}\ln 3 . \end{align*} \]

example.title: Calculating a Definite Integral of a Rational Function Using Partial Fractions

question.explanation:
First, we convert the integrand into a sum of partial fractions:

\begin{align*} \dfrac{2x-4}{x(x-4)}&= \dfrac{A}{x} +\dfrac{B}{x-4}, \end{align*}

which gives \[ 2x-4= A(x-4) +Bx. \]

Plugging in $x=4,$ we can eliminate $A$ and solve for $B\mathbin{:}$ \begin{align*} 2(4)-4 &= A(4-4) +B(4)\\[3pt] 4 &= 4B\\[3pt] 1 &= B \end{align*}

On the other hand, plugging in $x=0,$ we can eliminate $B$ and solve for $A\mathbin{:}$ \begin{align*} 2(0)-4&= A(0-4) +B(0)\\[3pt] -4 &= -4A\\[3pt] A&=1 \end{align*}

Therefore, \begin{align*} \dfrac{2x-4}{x(x-4)}&= \dfrac{1}{x} +\dfrac{1}{x-4}. \end{align*}

Finally, we integrate, and we get

\begin{align*} \int \dfrac{2x-4}{x(x-4)} \,\textrm{d}x &= \int \left( \dfrac{1}{x} + \dfrac{1}{x-4}\right) \textrm{d}x\\[5pt] &= \int \dfrac{1}{x} \,\textrm{d}x + \int \dfrac{1}{x-4}\, \textrm{d}x\\[5pt] &= \ln|x| + \ln |x-4 | + C. \end{align*}

example.title: Calculating an Indefinite Integral of a Rational Function Using Partial Fractions

question.text: Given that \[ \displaystyle \int \dfrac{x+15}{(x-3)(x+3)} \,\textrm{d}x= a\ln |x-3 | + b\ln|x+3| + C, \] find the value of $a+b.$
question.explanation:
First, we convert the integrand into a sum of partial fractions:

\begin{align*} \dfrac{x+15}{(x-3)(x+3)}& = \dfrac{A}{x-3} +\dfrac{B}{x+3}, \end{align*}

which gives \[ x+15 = A(x+3) +B(x-3). \]

Plugging in $x=-3,$ we can eliminate $A$ and solve for $B\mathbin{:}$ \begin{align*} -3+15 &= A(-3+3) +B(-3-3)\\[5pt] 12 &= -6 B\\[5pt] B &= -2 \end{align*}

On the other hand, plugging in $x=3,$ we can eliminate $B$ and solve for $A\mathbin{:}$ \begin{align*} 3+15 &= A(3+3) +B(3-3)\\[5pt] 18& = 6 A\\[5pt] A &= 3 \end{align*}

Therefore,

\begin{align*} \dfrac{x+15}{(x-3)(x+3)}& = \dfrac{3}{x-3} -\dfrac{2}{x+3}. \end{align*}

Finally, we integrate, and we get

\begin{align*} \int \dfrac{x+15}{(x-3)(x+3)} \,\textrm{d}x &= \int \left(\dfrac{3}{x-3} -\dfrac{2}{x+3}\right) \textrm{d}x\\[5pt] &= \int \dfrac{3}{x-3} \,\textrm{d}x - \int \dfrac{2}{x+3}\, \textrm{d}x\\[5pt] &= 3\ln |x-3 | - 2\ln|x+3| + C. \end{align*}

Finally, $a=3, b=-2,$ and $a+b = 3-2 = 1.$
